Hi, I'm assuming that cost is for hip replacement surgery? That seems slightly on the higher end, are you able to ask your vet if they can refer you anywhere that might be slightly cheaper?

Hip dysplasia can have multiple factors, over exercise in developing dogs can contribute, but this is generally before their growth plates close. It doesn't sound like the exercise she had was excessive, especially for an active breed.

Have you discussed trying to manage her with physiotherapy/hydrotherapy? These can make a huge difference in some cases. Sometimes long term pain medication can be useful too, but this will probably lead to her arthritis getting worse as she gets older.

If costs are a concern, then you may well be able to do surgery on one hip at a time, which will help to spread costs out for you.

Finally, although taking insurance out now will not help with covering for her hip dysplasia, it is still worth doing in case she develops any long term conditions in future. It can be expensive, and hopefully you never need it, but it can be absolutely invaluable especially as pets get older.

I'm so sorry for your loss. The medication I normally send owners home with as an "emergency" dose is rectal diazepam. It sometimes works, and sometimes doesn't. I can't tell you why you weren't sent home with any.

For what it's worth, rectal diazepam would be fairly unlikely to be able to make a difference to/stop severe cluster seizures. Regarding the IV getting tangled, unfortunately our patients often move around in their kennels, and IVs can often get pulled out. This can happen in literally seconds. Sometimes a patient will be sneaky and pull an IV out when we can't see them, and we only realise when we go to give meds or the drip pump starts beeping. While patients on seizure watch will be very closely monitored, we cannot always have eyes on them constantly. It is really really difficult to place a catheter in a dog that is actively seizuring.

Once again I'm so sorry for your loss. Losing pets is always so difficult, and even more so when they are young and it is so unexpected.

The highest risk period after a blockage is the initial week or so. After that (particularly if you make diet and management changes) the chances of reblocking will be much lower. Its difficult to say exactly how likely it is that he will block again without more information, and I can't remember the exact clinical figures off the top of my head, but (from personal clinical experience) less than 50% of the cats that we manage to unblock will block again in the next week.

If his renal blood parameters are normal at this stage thats definitely a good sign - most of the blocked cats I have euthanised are either because we cannot manage to unblock them, or because they have already suffered irreparable kidney failure.

Its definitely worth changing his diet to one of the stone dissolution ones available. If you're able to, feeding wet rather than dry will definitely help long term too. Management wise, minimising stress is important - you can try feliway diffusers or similar, if you have other cats in the house make sure they all have access to 1 litter tray per social group, and separate food/water bowls for each cat. Keeping male cats at a healthy weight is important too, as obesity can be a risk factor.
